cmimc-2024-mathdash-02.title: Count faces
cmimc-2024-mathdash-02.body:
The four original faces each remain (as hexagons, with the corners removed). Each cut adds one new triangular face, and there are four corners, so $4$ new faces. Total $4+4=8$ (a truncated tetrahedron).

**Answer: $8$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-03.title: Inclusion-exclusion
cmimc-2024-mathdash-03.body:
Divisible by $2$ and $3$ means divisible by $6$: $\lfloor1000/6\rfloor=166$ numbers. Those also divisible by $5$ are divisible by $30$: $\lfloor1000/30\rfloor=33$. So $166-33=133$.

**Answer: $133$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-05.title: Case on where I sits
cmimc-2024-mathdash-05.body:
The letter $I$ must not have two different neighbors.

- $I$ at an end (positions $1$ or $5$): it has one neighbor, so any arrangement of $C,C,M,M$ in the other four places works: $\binom42=6$ each, giving $12$.
- $I$ in positions $2,3,4$: both neighbors must be the same letter. If both are $C$, the remaining two spots get $M,M$: $1$ way; similarly both $M$: $1$ way. That is $2$ ways for each of $3$ positions, giving $6$.

Total $12+6=18$.

**Answer: $18$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-05.title: Check
cmimc-2024-mathdash-05.body:
Enumerating all $30$ distinct arrangements of CMIMC and counting those where $I$'s neighbors are not two different letters gives $18$.

**Answer: $18$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-06.title: Self-similarity
cmimc-2024-mathdash-06.body:
Let $t=2+\cfrac{2}{2+\cfrac2{2+\cdots}}$. Then $t=2+\frac2t$, so $t^2-2t-2=0$ and $t=1+\sqrt3$. The given number is $1+\frac2t=1+\frac{2}{1+\sqrt3}=1+(\sqrt3-1)=\sqrt3=0+\sqrt3$. So $a=0$, $b=3$ and $a+b=3$.

**Answer: $3$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-07.title: Distance to the hypotenuse
cmimc-2024-mathdash-07.body:
Put $B=(0,0)$, $A=(15,0)$, $C=(0,8)$, so $AC=17$. The semicircle has diameter along $AB$ starting at $B$, so its center is $O=(r,0)$ and it is automatically tangent to $BC$. Tangency to $AC$ (line $8x+15y=120$) means $\frac{|8r-120|}{17}=r$, so $120-8r=17r$ and $r=\frac{24}5$. Hence $a+b=24+5=29$.

**Answer: $29$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-07.title: Tangent lengths
cmimc-2024-mathdash-07.body:
The circle is tangent to $BC$ at $B$ and to $AC$ at some point $T$, so $CT=CB=8$ and $AT=17-8=9$. Also $AO=15-r$ and $\triangle ATO\sim\triangle ABC$ (right angle at $T$): $\frac{r}{AT}=\frac{BC}{AB}$, so $r=9\cdot\frac8{15}=\frac{24}5$.

**Answer: $29$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-08.title: Odd double factorial
cmimc-2024-mathdash-08.body:
$2024!$ is the product of the even numbers up to $2024$, which equals $2^{1012}\cdot1012!$, times the product of the odd numbers up to $2023$. So the quotient is $1\cdot3\cdot5\cdots2023$. This product is odd and divisible by $5$, so it ends in $5$.

**Answer: $5$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-09.title: Clear denominators
cmimc-2024-mathdash-09.body:
Multiplying by $x(x+1)(x+2)$: $x(x+2)+x(x+1)=(x+1)(x+2)$, i.e. $2x^2+3x=x^2+3x+2$, so $x^2=2$ and $x=\pm\sqrt2$ (neither makes a denominator zero). The product is $-2$.

**Answer: $-2$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-10.title: Compute the triangle
cmimc-2024-mathdash-10.body:
Arc $AB$ is $120^\circ$. $C$ is the arc midpoint, so $OC\perp AB$ and line $CD$ (perpendicular to $AB$ through $C$) is the line $CO$, meeting $AB$ at its midpoint $E$. $AB=2\cdot8\sin60^\circ=8\sqrt3$, so $BE=4\sqrt3$. The distance from $O$ to $AB$ is $8\cos60^\circ=4$, so $CE=8-4=4$. Triangle $CBE$ is right-angled at $E$ with area $\frac12\cdot4\sqrt3\cdot4=8\sqrt3$, and its square is $192$.

**Answer: $192$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-11.title: Sum over head counts
cmimc-2024-mathdash-11.body:
$P(A=k)=\frac{\binom2k}4$, $P(B=k)=\frac{\binom4k}{16}$. The probability of equal head counts is $\frac{1\cdot1+2\cdot4+1\cdot6}{64}=\frac{15}{64}$. So $m+n=15+64=79$.

**Answer: $79$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-12.title: Rewrite f
cmimc-2024-mathdash-12.body:
Substituting $x\mapsto y/3$: $f(y)=\frac{y^2}9+\frac y3+1$. Then $f\!\left(\frac z3\right)=\frac{z^2}{81}+\frac z9+1=7$ gives $z^2+9z-486=0$. Its roots are real (discriminant $81+1944>0$), and their sum is $-9$.

**Answer: $-9$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-13.title: Similar triangles
cmimc-2024-mathdash-13.body:
$ANPM$ is a parallelogram, so $NP=AM$ and $MP=AN$. $\angle A=\angle MAN=91^\circ$, so in $\triangle AMN$, $\angle ANM=180^\circ-91^\circ-47^\circ=42^\circ$ and $\angle C=180^\circ-91^\circ-42^\circ=47^\circ$. Thus $\triangle AMN\sim\triangle ACB$ (the angles $91^\circ,47^\circ,42^\circ$ at $A,M,N$ correspond to those at $A,C,B$), hence $\frac{AM}{AC}=\frac{AN}{AB}$.

Since $MP\parallel AB$: $\frac{CP}{CB}=\frac{MP}{AB}=\frac{AN}{AB}$; since $NP\parallel AC$: $\frac{BP}{BC}=\frac{NP}{AC}=\frac{AM}{AC}$. These ratios are equal because $\frac{AM}{AC}=\frac{AN}{AB}$, and they sum to $1$, so each is $\frac12$. Hence $P$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $\frac{CB}{BP}=2$.

**Answer: $2$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-14.title: Congruences
cmimc-2024-mathdash-14.body:
The last digit in base $b$ is the remainder mod $b$, so $n\equiv7\pmod 8$, $\pmod{10}$, $\pmod{12}$, i.e. $n\equiv7\pmod{120}$ ($\operatorname{lcm}(8,10,12)=120$). In $[300,400]$ the only such $n$ is $7+3\cdot120=367$.

**Answer: $367$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-15.title: Find k
cmimc-2024-mathdash-15.body:
Substituting $x=3$: $27-9k+60-15=0$, so $k=8$. The roots sum to $k=8$ by Vieta, so the other two roots sum to $8-3=5$. (Indeed $x^3-8x^2+20x-15=(x-3)(x^2-5x+5)$.) Since $k$ is forced, the only possible sum, hence the greatest, is $5$.

**Answer: $5$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-16.title: Cauchy-Schwarz
cmimc-2024-mathdash-16.body:
Let $x_1,\dots,x_4$ be the four denominators; all are positive for a quadrilateral, and $\sum x_i=2(a+b+c+d)$. Then the left side is $\frac12\left(\sum\frac1{x_i}\right)\left(\sum x_i\right)\ge\frac12\cdot16=8$ by Cauchy-Schwarz (AM-HM), with equality iff all $x_i$ are equal, i.e. $a=b=c=d$. A square is cyclic, so the bound $8$ is attained and $K=8$.

**Answer: $8$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-17.title: Track the count
cmimc-2024-mathdash-17.body:
With $n$ tiles, exactly $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ are perfect squares, so $n\mapsto n-\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. Iterating from $2024$ gives $2024,1980,1936,1892,1849,1806,1764,1722,\dots$; each value of $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor=m$ lasts about two steps (the interval $[m^2,(m+1)^2)$ has $2m+1$ numbers and we subtract $m$ each time), so roughly $2$ steps per value of $m$ from $44$ down to $1$. Carrying the iteration to the end (the last terms are $\dots,20,16,12,9,6,4,2,1$) gives $88$ operations in total.

**Answer: $88$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-17.title: Computation
cmimc-2024-mathdash-17.body:
Starting at $2024$ and repeatedly replacing $n$ by $n-\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ until $n=1$ takes exactly $88$ steps.

**Answer: $88$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-18.title: Complex numbers
cmimc-2024-mathdash-18.body:
The circumradius is $\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt3}=1$. Place $O$ at the origin and $A,B,C$ at the cube roots of unity. For $P=z$, $AP\cdot BP\cdot CP=|z-1||z-\omega||z-\omega^2|=|z^3-1|=7$. Let $w=z^3$: $|w-1|=7$ allows $|w|$ to be any value in $[6,8]$ (with $w=-6$ and $w=8$ at the extremes). Since $OP^3=|w|$, $OP^3\in[6,8]$: $x^3=8$, $y^3=6$. So $x^6-y^6=64-36=28$.

**Answer: $28$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-19.title: Recurrence on compositions
cmimc-2024-mathdash-19.body:
The allowed parts are $1,2,3,5,8$ (the Fibonacci numbers up to $10$). Let $w(n)$ be the number of ordered sums for $n$ (with $w(0)=1$). Then $w(n)=w(n-1)+w(n-2)+w(n-3)+w(n-5)+w(n-8)$ with terms with negative index omitted. This gives $w(1),\dots,w(10)=1,2,4,7,14,26,49,94,177,336$. (Check: $w(3)=4$ as in the example.)

**Answer: $336$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-20.title: Sicherman dice
cmimc-2024-mathdash-20.body:
The generating function of a die is $A(x)=\sum x^{a_i}$, and we need $A(x)B(x)=(x+x^2+\dots+x^6)^2=x^2\big[(1+x)(1+x+x^2)(1-x+x^2)\big]^2$. The factors $1+x$, $1+x+x^2$, $1-x+x^2$ are irreducible over $\mathbb Z$ and take the values $2,3,1$ at $x=1$. Since $A(1)=B(1)=6$, each of $A,B$ contains exactly one factor $(1+x)$ and one factor $(1+x+x^2)$, and the two copies of $(1-x+x^2)$ are split as $(1,1)$ or $(0,2)$. Positive faces force each to carry a factor $x$.

- Split $(1,1)$: both are the standard die, faces summing to $21$.
- Split $(0,2)$: $A=x(1+x)(1+x+x^2)=x+2x^2+2x^3+x^4$ (faces $1,2,2,3,3,4$, sum $15$) and $B=x(1+x)(1+x+x^2)(1-x+x^2)^2=x+x^3+x^4+x^5+x^6+x^8$ (faces $1,3,4,5,6,8$, sum $27$).

So the greatest possible sum on one cube is $27$.

**Answer: $27$**

cmimc-2024-mathdash-20.title: Search
cmimc-2024-mathdash-20.body:
Exhaustively checking all pairs of $6$-multisets of positive integers whose pairwise sums reproduce the distribution finds only the standard pair and the Sicherman pair, with face sums $(21,21)$ and $(15,27)$.

**Answer: $27$**
